newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's fake quake sets off political tremors.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's fake quake sets off political tremors.

text.p: The Portuguese government should abandon a plan to simulate an earthquake by detonating 20 tonnes of explosives under the sea, a leading geophysics professor said on Tuesday.
The plan, known as "Operation Combo", has set off political tremors in Portugal, haunted by a 1755 earthquake that killed 40,000 people and reduced the capital Lisbon to rubble.
Citizens in the northern coastal area are worried about the blast and environmental groups have protested, saying it could destroy up to 280 square km (110 square miles) of marine life.

Professor Joao Montenegro of Oporto University's Geophysics Institute said the government should drop the plan, part of an international experiment to monitor seismic impact, because it could set off a real earthquake.

"We have no means of calculating what will happen," Montenegro told a news conference. "It's like a patient who takes a little arsenic to help him lose weight. If he accidentally takes too much he will die."
Scientists in the project say the only visible sign of the underwater explosion will be the appearance of dark patches on the sea surface.
They say people in high-rise apartments may feel a slight tremor, but the effect on buildings should be no more serious than that of a heavy truck passing on a nearby road.
"Operation Combo" is due off the coast of Oporto in northern Portugal before mid-November but the exact time and location have been kept secret to avoid public alarm.

Northern politicians, outraged that the Lisbon government agreed to dropping 20 tonnes of high explosives in their backyard, recently pushed a protest vote through parliament, forcing authorities to reconsider the plan.
Planning Minister Joao Cravinho has said he will announce a decision shortly on whether to go ahead with the project which has already been postponed twice.

One environmentalist group, known as the "Amigos do Mar" ("Friends of the Sea"), suggested the scientists use a giant cylinder with a hammer contraption built inside to set off the same seismic waves without killing millions of fish.
The Lisbon earthquake on All Saints' Day, 1755 was followed by a huge tidal wave and fires. Historical records say that 30,000 people were killed within six minutes.
Portugal's most recent serious earthquake occurred in 1980 in the mid-Atlantic Azores islands. It killed 43 people and left hundreds injured.
